title: The Backup Plan That Ran for 142 Years
subtitle: A sea captain sailed 171 days around Cape Horn looking for the perfect mill site, lost his first choice to a rival, and settled on a sandspit that outlasted almost everything built after it.
sed: A sea captain sailed 171 days around Cape Horn looking for the perfect mill site, lost his first choice to a rival, and settled on a sandspit that…

attrs.alt: The Port Gamble mill waterfront around 1900, with sailing ships at the wharf

content.text: Port Gamble around 1900, from a Seattle promotional brochure compiled by Alfred D. Bowen.
Public domain
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Drive up the Kitsap Peninsula toward Hood Canal and you'll pass through a town that looks like someone airlifted a slice of coastal New England onto Puget Sound and forgot to change it back. That's not an accident. Port Gamble was built by New Englanders, for New Englanders, and for 142 years it did one thing without stopping: cut lumber.
The town's whole existence traces back to a captain who almost built it somewhere else.
A Long Way to Find a Sandspit

In July 1853, William C. Talbot anchored the schooner Julius Pringle in Discovery Bay and set out in a small sailboat to explore Hood Canal, hunting for a place to put a sawmill. Getting there had not been quick. Talbot had captained the 50-ton Julius Pringle from his hometown of East Machias, Maine, all the way around Cape Horn to Puget Sound — a voyage of 171 days.

His first choice was Port Ludlow. It had everything he wanted, and someone else had already claimed it. So he kept looking, and found a sandspit at the mouth of a two-mile bay: sheltered from the prevailing winds, ringed with Douglas fir, with room enough for a mill and the buildings around it. Good enough to become, almost by default, the site of the longest continuously running sawmill in American history.
A Place That Already Had a Name

The spit wasn't empty when Talbot found it. S'Klallam families lived there and on the bluff above, and they called the place Teekalet — brightness of the noonday sun. Talbot borrowed the name for his mill. His partner, Josiah Keller, later persuaded the S'Klallam to move across the bay to Point Julia, in exchange for free lumber, firewood, and Christmas gifts. Many of them went to work at the mill, commuting to the job site by canoe.
Building It From Scratch

Talbot landed ten men, most of them from East Machias, and they threw up a bunkhouse, a cookhouse, and a store before touching the mill itself. The actual machinery arrived separately, aboard the clipper schooner L.P. Foster, along with Keller, who took charge of the operation once he landed. Within a week of getting the engine, boilers, and a single-blade muley saw ashore, the crew had steam up and cut their first log — by September 1853. Early output ran around 2,000 board feet a day, roughly a tenth of what a five-room house of the era required.

Here's the detail worth holding onto: Talbot's very first Puget Sound lumber shipment didn't come from his own mill at all. That same September, before his mill's machinery had even arrived, he bought pilings from Henry Yesler in Seattle.
A Company Town, Paid in Fifty-Cent Pieces

The town that grew up on the spit was pure transplanted New England, right down to its habits. Workers earned about $30 a month, paid so reliably in fifty-cent pieces that "four bit" coins became a kind of badge of Port Gamble employment. In 1859 the company built the first school in Kitsap County. The settlement itself didn't take the name Port Gamble until 1868, honoring a Navy lieutenant wounded in the War of 1812.
The Mill That Didn't Stop
The mill's last 20 workers reported for their final day on November 30, 1995 — 142 continuous years after that first cut, and the longest run of any sawmill in the United States.
If You Go

The Port Gamble townsite sits on the Kitsap Peninsula at the mouth of Hood Canal and has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1966. You can still walk the whole story: the general store, the 1879 church, and the Walker-Ames House up on the bluff all survived the mill's closing. Across the bay at Point Julia, the Port Gamble S'Klallam Tribe lives on the water its ancestors never really left.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: One Acre, Returned
subtitle: In 1870 the federal government ordered a Suquamish longhouse destroyed. It took 134 years, a sale made out of poverty, and a unanimous vote for the state to hand even one acre of it back.
sed: In 1870 the federal government ordered a Suquamish longhouse destroyed. It took 134 years, a sale made out of poverty, and a unanimous vote for the…

attrs.alt: Old Man House Park at Suquamish, a grassy shoreline park on Agate Passage

content.text: Old Man House Park at Suquamish, 2020. Photo: Rachel Robnett,
CC BY-SA 4.0
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Cross the Agate Passage bridge onto the Kitsap Peninsula and you're a short drive from a one-acre beach park that doesn't look like much. No plaque towering over the parking lot, no gift shop. But that acre carries one of the more difficult, and more instructive, stories in Puget Sound history — one of erasure, and then, remarkably, of return.
A Longhouse Big Enough to Hold a Village

Old Man House stood on the beach at Suquamish, directly across Agate Passage from the north end of Bainbridge Island. It was the winter village of the Suquamish and the home of both Chief Seattle and Chief Kitsap. Accounts of its exact size differ — HistoryLink puts it at roughly 900 feet long and 60 feet wide, divided into 40 apartments, while the Suquamish Museum simply calls it the largest longhouse in the region. Either way, this wasn't a single family's home. It was a center of communal life.

In 1870, federal officials ordered it destroyed. The official reason given was public health. The actual effect was assimilation — communal living was exactly what federal policy of that era was designed to break apart, and tearing down the house did it.
You should sit with that for a moment before moving on. It's the hinge the rest of this story turns on.
Leaving the Land Without Leaving It

The Suquamish kept living on the ground where Old Man House had stood until 1904, when they were pushed onto individual family allotments. That same year, poor and squeezed, the tribe sold the beach itself to the U.S. Army. Developers owned it after that. In 1950 it became Old Man House State Park — one acre of shell-strewn sand, all that remained in public memory of what had once stood there. Park signs updated in 1975 described the Suquamish as people who "once lived in the area."
They had never left.
A Vote, and a Recess

On August 12, 2004, the Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission voted to give that one acre to the Suquamish Tribe. It was the first time the state had ever given land to a tribe. The seven-member commission's decision was unanimous, though it came with conditions: the tribe agreed to spend $50,000 over five years on maintenance, and the state kept the right to take the park back if the land were ever privatized or the park's hours and other conditions ignored.

Not everyone in town wanted it to happen. One neighborhood group fought the transfer; another worked alongside the tribe to see it through. Reverend Tom Thresher of the Suquamish Community Congregational United Church of Christ told the commission, "You have an opportunity to heal old wounds, and I think reach out a hand in friendship today that I think will heal our community." Rob Purser, the tribal member who led the effort, called it "a good step in the healing process for the tribe."
When the vote came down, the commission had to recess. Tribal members sang a song of thanks and drummed. About twenty Suquamish who had arrived by canoe beat their paddles on the floor.
What's There Now

Old Man House Park is still there, at 17818 South Angeline Avenue NE in Suquamish — one acre of beach, returned. Nearby stands the House of Awakened Culture, dedicated in February 2009 and built to honor the longhouse that had been destroyed. It was the first traditional communal space the Suquamish had had in 139 years. Chief Seattle's grave is in the Suquamish cemetery, where a graveside ceremony each August anchors Chief Seattle Days, held in town since 1911.
If You Go

Old Man House Park sits at 17818 South Angeline Avenue NE, Suquamish, WA — near the House of Awakened Culture and Chief Seattle's grave in the Suquamish cemetery. Treat it as the tribe's living history that it is: a place to walk respectfully, not a roadside attraction. Chief Seattle Days, held in town each August, is the most visible time to understand what this ground means to the people who fought to get it back.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: The Piano on the Hill
subtitle: A wartime neighborhood that became Bremerton's de facto housing for Black shipyard workers was gone within a few years of the war's end. What one boy found on its community-center stage wasn't.
sed: A wartime neighborhood that became Bremerton's de facto housing for Black shipyard workers was gone within a few years of the war's end. What one boy…

attrs.alt: The aircraft carrier USS Saratoga off the Puget Sound Navy Yard in 1942

content.text: USS Saratoga off the Puget Sound Navy Yard, May 14, 1942, during the wartime build-up that brought workers to Bremerton. U.S. Navy photo,
Public domain
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Much of the hill west of downtown Bremerton is car dealerships today. But for about five years in the 1940s, this hilltop held a crowded wartime neighborhood that mattered far more than its size — and it produced Quincy Jones.
A City That Outgrew Itself

Bremerton's 1940 census counted seven Black residents. By 1945 it had more than 4,500. The pull was the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard, ramping up after Pearl Harbor and desperate for workers. Federal policy did not require segregated housing, and the nine developments built around Bremerton and Port Orchard to handle the influx were planned as integrated. Then some white residents in those developments objected to Black neighbors, and the Bremerton Housing Authority made one project the de facto development for Black families and assigned most new arrivals there: Sinclair Park, 280 prefabricated units spread across 80 acres on a hill west of Bremerton, named for nearby Sinclair Inlet. People called it Sinclair Heights.

By August 1944, the housing authority's own count showed 342 Black families in its care. Two hundred seventy-nine of them lived in Sinclair Park. Of the development's 280 units, 279 held Black families. The last one held a Filipino family.
Life on the Hill

It was not an easy place to live. Construction started in the summer of 1942, and the first residents — Eugene Aires and Elwood Greer — moved in that March of 1943. There was no landscaping. There were no streetlights at first, and longtime residents remembered the darkness for decades afterward. The neighborhood sat a mile outside the school district, far enough that the bus wouldn't come up the hill. Until a phone booth was added, the development had exactly one telephone, and it was in the community center.

That community center is where this story turns. Built in 1943 for about $57,000, it was one of the first buildings designed by a young Seattle architecture firm called Naramore, Bain, Brady and Johanson — the firm that would later become NBBJ, one of the largest architecture practices in the world. Inside, volunteers ran a night library twice a week. Voting booths went up there at election time. Lilian Walker started Bremerton's NAACP branch inside its walls. A drama club staged a production called "Jiving Macbeth" on its small stage.
The Boy and the Piano
On that stage sat an upright piano. An eleven-year-old boy broke into the building with some friends to steal a pie, wandered into the recreation room, and found it waiting for him.
"I went up there, paused, stared, and then tinkled on it for a moment," he wrote years later. "That's where I began to find peace."
The boy was Quincy Jones. He kept sneaking back until a sympathetic supervisor started leaving the door unlocked for him.

It is worth sitting with that for a second. One of the most influential musicians of the twentieth century found his way to a piano because he'd broken into a segregated wartime community center to steal food. That's rather the point of a neighborhood like this one — it held whole lives inside a system that sorted them onto one hill, and sometimes those lives went on to reshape American music.
Built to Disappear

Sinclair Heights was never meant to last. The houses were built from panels that were easy to take down. Eighty units went up for sale on July 1, 1946, and by 1948 the rest were gone — some of them floated down to waterfront lots around the Kitsap Peninsula and turned into summer cabins. What remained was streets, sidewalks, and the community center, which went on to serve as a National Guard armory until it was torn down in late 2002.
What's Left

Much of the hilltop is car dealerships today; the community center's footprint is now an emergency-services training center. But the story has found its way back downtown. Quincy Square, with a woven bronze sculpture of Jones's face, opened on Fourth Street on July 12, 2025, three blocks up from the Bremerton ferry terminal; interpretive signs on Jones's early life and Sinclair Heights followed. And in the lobby of the Kitsap History Museum stands a scuffed Melville Clark upright piano, said to be the one from the hill. Nobody has roped it off. You can put your hands on the keys.

A neighborhood built to be temporary, and torn down on schedule, still managed to leave something behind that a city built a square around. That is the strange arithmetic of a place like Sinclair Heights: designed to disappear, and it mostly did, except for the one thing that mattered most.
If You Go
Quincy Square

— Fourth Street, downtown Bremerton, a few blocks from the Bremerton ferry terminal. Look for the woven bronze sculpture of Jones's face and the interpretive signs on his early life and Sinclair Heights.
Kitsap History Museum
— downtown Bremerton. The piano attributed to the Sinclair Park community center stands in the lobby, unroped. Check current hours before you go.
The original hilltop site, west of downtown, is now largely car dealerships; the community center's footprint is an emergency-services training center.

This is sensitive ground — a story about segregation carried out by a local housing authority's assignments rather than by law, in a city that badly needed the workers it was mistreating. It deserves to be told plainly, without smoothing over the parts that are hard to sit with. That the story ends with a sculpture doesn't undo what came before it.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: The Ferry Dock That Wouldn't Retire
subtitle: A fisherman's 1949 beach landing on Hood Canal carried ferries until the bridge opened in 1961. The state has come back for it twice since — once when the bridge sank, once when it rebuilt the other half.
sed: A fisherman's 1949 beach landing on Hood Canal carried ferries until the bridge opened in 1961. The state has come back for it twice since — once when…

attrs.alt: Looking west along the Hood Canal Bridge from its east end

content.text: The Hood Canal Bridge from its east end, 2021. Photo: SounderBruce,
CC BY-SA 4.0
, via Wikimedia Commons.

On August 12, 1961, thousands of people sat in a five-mile traffic backup on Hood Canal, waiting to drive across a brand-new bridge that was opening fifteen months behind schedule. The floating section ran 6,520 feet across 23 concrete pontoons — the longest bridge of its kind in the world, and the first one anyone had tried to float on salt water with tides that rise and fall dramatically over the course of a day.

At the end of a road called Wesley Way sits a quiet private dock. That little beach landing has carried the state's ferry traffic in three separate stretches — a regular run in the 1950s, then twice more when the bridge was out — and it started out as one fisherman's side project.
A Fisherman's Dock

Bill Lofall was a commercial fisherman. He and his wife Martha owned a stretch of Hood Canal beach property, and in 1949 the Black Ball Line — a private ferry operator — asked to put a landing on it. Bill built the dock and the access road, which still carries the name Wesley Way. Black Ball supplied the pilings and mechanical gear. The landing was commissioned on June 10, 1950, and within a year the state had taken over Black Ball's Puget Sound ferry routes entirely.
Three Buildings, One Crossing

The crossing needed more than a dock. A ferry waiting room went up, with a single office inside. A bait house let Bill and Martha sell herring to the local fishing fleet. And Bill barged in a building from Scandia and set it up as a restaurant, the Sea Breeze Inn, where Ruth Ryan sold hot food to travelers waiting for the next boat. Her husband Red ran the tavern and gas station at the Lofall four corners nearby.
The Boats That Came and Went

Four vessels worked the run over its eleven years. The wooden ferry Kitsap, good for about 30 cars, stayed on the route the entire time. The wooden Vashon made 28 crossings a day until 1954. The Olympic filled in for about a month, from March to April 1954. Then came the Rhododendron — originally the Gov. Herbert R. O'Conner on Chesapeake Bay, retired there when a bridge put her out of work, then bought by Washington State, towed through the Panama Canal, and renamed for the state flower. The crossing itself took about ten minutes.
Retired, Then Recommissioned — Twice

When the Hood Canal Bridge opened in 1961, the ferry run was retired and the Lofalls got their property back. The old waiting room and the Sea Breeze Inn became rental houses. In 1973, the Lofall Community Corporation was formed to buy the site.

Six years after that, on the morning of February 13, 1979, the western half of the Hood Canal Bridge broke loose in a windstorm and sank. The state came looking for Lofall again. WSDOT built a long pier for a passenger-only run to South Point on the Jefferson County side, then modified the main dock to land car ferries. The rebuilt bridge reopened on October 3, 1982. Then in 2009, when the bridge's aging east half was replaced and the bridge closed for six weeks, the state came back a third time: a passenger water shuttle ran between the Lofall dock and South Point, with buses to park-and-ride lots on each side.
What's There Now
The dock itself is private property. If you want a public place to stop, Salsbury Point Park, a Kitsap County park one mile west of Port Gamble, has its own dock in the water from April to October.

There's something almost funny about it, if you squint: the state builds an enormous, record-setting bridge that makes a little beach ferry obsolete, and then spends the next several decades occasionally needing that same beach back. Hood Canal has a way of humbling infrastructure. The dock at Lofall just happened to be standing there each time it did.
If You Go
Wesley Way, Lofall
— the access road Bill Lofall built still runs down to the dock. The dock is private property.
Salsbury Point Park
— 3160 NW Wheeler Street, Poulsbo, one mile west of Port Gamble. Kitsap County park; its dock is in from April to October.
The Hood Canal Bridge carries SR 104 across the canal and is a straightforward stop if you're already touring North Kitsap.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: The Port That Only Ever Wanted a Beach
subtitle: In 1919, eleven voters on the north Kitsap shore created a public port district to own a single dock. The dock is long gone. The port — and its refusal to grow into anything more — is still there.
sed: In 1919, eleven voters on the north Kitsap shore created a public port district to own a single dock. The dock is long gone. The port — and its refusal…

attrs.alt: A steamer tied up at the end of a long wooden wharf at Suquamish in 1911

content.text: The steamer Kitsap at the wharf in Suquamish, June 1911, in the Mosquito Fleet era.
Public domain
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Drive north from Kingston on the east side of the Kitsap Peninsula and you'll pass Eglon without much warning — a scatter of houses above a beach, three miles short of Point No Point. There's no sign announcing what happened here, because nothing announces it. But on August 30, 1919, a bill of sale changed hands in this small settlement for exactly one dollar, and the wooden dock it transferred became the reason for one of the stubbornest little governments in Washington State.
A Name That Was Second Choice

Families started settling here in the early 1900s, along a small creek named for homesteaders Charles and Jessie Silver. They called the place Silver Creek, and it might have stayed Silver Creek if the name hadn't already been taken by another Washington community when residents applied for their own post office in 1906. They needed something else. They chose Eglon, out of the Old Testament — the story goes it won because it was the shortest of three names on the list.
Getting Here Meant Getting Wet

Before there was a dock, there was rowing. Mosquito Fleet steamers passed the Eglon beach several times a day on their runs between Seattle and the small towns around the sound, but with nothing to tie up to, someone had to row out and meet them. In decent weather that worked well enough to move a passenger or some light cargo. In bad weather, you stayed aboard and tried again the next day. Livestock didn't get the rowboat treatment — they were swum ashore, or herded up the beach from Kingston on foot.

Residents built their first real dock in 1913, through the Eglon Dock Company. It didn't last: by 1918, upkeep had fallen to too few volunteers, the structure was unsafe, and the community tore it down to start over. A private Community Dock Company put up a replacement that same fall, and the Puget Sound Navigation Company announced that starting November 10, 1918, "the Steamer PUGET will land at the new dock in Eglon in both directions."
Eleven Voters and a Dollar

Even before the new dock was built, the community had turned to the harder question of how to keep one maintained. On July 12, 1919, eleven registered voters turned out to decide whether to form a public port district — and ten said yes. Gust Sevon, Nikolai Naykki, and Henry Johnson became the first port commissioners. The county canvassed the vote on July 21, and about six weeks later, on August 30, the dock passed to the new Port of Eglon for that famous single dollar. Naykki took the paid job of wharfinger, dock manager — though the position came with a catch: out of his own salary, he had to buy the coal oil that kept the dock's night light burning.
The Dock Disappeared. The Port Didn't.

Progress caught up with Eglon fast. The first car ferry ran from Kingston in 1923. The county highway reached the community in 1924. Scheduled boat service to the dock ended by 1933, and the dock itself came down by the early 1940s. By 1940 the port had even stopped collecting taxes — its last real expenditure for years was fifty dollars spent on lumber for a beach bathhouse in 1945.
What the Port of Eglon would not do, through any of this, was dissolve.

In 1960, the state legislature floated a plan to fold Washington's many small port districts into one statewide authority. Port of Eglon commissioner George Coles put his community's position plainly: "We don't want any industry," he said. "Leave us alone. We don't want to be infringed upon. We want to keep our little bit of beach and use it for the children to swim." At the time, Kitsap County had twenty-one separate port districts — more than any other county in the state. By 2011 that number had shrunk to twelve through voluntary consolidations and dissolutions, and Kitsap still held the record.
The statewide consolidation plan died. Eglon's port did not.
What's Left

Go north from Kingston today and you can still park above the beach, launch a boat for free, and sit at a picnic table beside a fire pit on the hundred feet of shoreline the port kept after the steamers stopped calling. Neighbors still gather there on Wednesday nights all through the summer. It isn't much of a port, in the sense that word usually means — no industry, no development, no growth. That was always exactly the point.
If You Go
Port of Eglon boat launch
, Eglon (north of Kingston). Free boat launch, a parking lot, and a picnic area with tables, a picnic shelter, and a fire pit.

The Wednesday evening gatherings through the summer are a longstanding neighborhood tradition — a good reason to time a visit for one, but worth remembering it's a community gathering place, not a public event.
There's no dock left to see — that's the point of the story. What you're visiting is the hundred feet of beach the port fought to keep instead.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: Lunch at 800 Feet, Days Before It Came Down
subtitle: In 1972, three Bainbridge Island parks officials climbed the tallest thing on the island one last time — and ate their sandwiches at the top before the Navy's secret tower was torn apart for scrap.
sed: In 1972, three Bainbridge Island parks officials climbed the tallest thing on the island one last time — and ate their sandwiches at the top before the…

attrs.alt: The Ritchie Observatory doors at Battle Point Park with a large ceramic transmitter insulator in front

content.text: The Edwin E. Ritchie Observatory at Battle Point Park, with an insulator from the site's wartime Navy transmitter out front. Photo: Dicklyon,
CC BY-SA 4.0
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Walk into Battle Point Park today and you'll pass through two stone pillars with wartime fencing still attached to them, on your way to a playground, ballfields, and a telescope open to the public. None of it gives away what stood here for most of three decades: the tallest structure on Bainbridge Island, and a secret almost nobody on the island was supposed to know.
One Last Climb

In 1972, three men from the Bainbridge Island parks district — director Dennis McCurdy, assistant director Larry Burris, and commissioner Fred Grimm — climbed an 800-foot steel tower at Battle Point and sat down at the top to eat lunch. They knew it was their last chance. The tower was scheduled to come down within days. The climb up took them about 90 minutes. Coming down took half an hour.
Why the Tower Was There

The Navy built a radio transmitter station at Battle Point in September 1942, north of Fort Ward. Fort Ward was the secret listening post, intercepting Tokyo's radio traffic; Battle Point's job, per HistoryLink, was relaying messages from the Pacific to the 13th Naval Command in Seattle. The station included a reinforced concrete transmitter building, a helix building, and four 300-foot towers — the 800-footer came later, and was for years the tallest thing on the island. The stone pillars and fencing still standing at the park entrance today were built during the war specifically to keep people away from all of it.
The Towers Come Down

The Navy shut Battle Point down in 1971, and the ground passed to the Bainbridge Island Metropolitan Park & Recreation District, which took formal title to more than 90 acres on May 5, 1972. Part of the deal: the towers had to go. Locals had long regarded the big one as a "terrible temptation to climb," and that year 311 tons of steel came down, hauled away by a contractor who got to keep the scrap in exchange for the work. The 864th Engineer Battalion, out of Fort Lewis, then graded the site as a training exercise — work that saved the parks district an estimated $100,000.
The buildings, unlike the towers, were left standing.
From Helix House to Observatory

In 1992, Edwin Ritchie, John Rudolph, and Mac Gardiner founded the Battle Point Astronomical Association and turned their attention to the abandoned Helix House — a 26-by-38-foot building with 25-foot walls that had once housed the coil generating the long carrier waves sent out to the fleet. The parks district was planning to tear it down. The new association talked the district out of it.

Gardiner, a retired Boeing engineer, tracked down a 27.5-inch Zerodur mirror, surplus from a discontinued Strategic Defense Initiative program. Rudolph, an architect, drew up the renovation plans and ran the volunteer construction crew. Ritchie, a machinist and prosthetic-limb designer by trade, machined nearly all of the telescope himself, bending its steel fork mount into shape with a 20-ton press. He died on March 13, 1997, not long after finishing the work. The Edwin E. Ritchie Observatory was dedicated that December 21.
What's There Now

Visit Battle Point Park at 10800 Battle Point Drive NE and the war is still visible if you know where to look. The old transmitter building now hosts gymnastics classes. The Helix House holds the largest telescope open to the public in the Pacific Northwest, under a 17-foot plywood dome the volunteers built themselves. The Battle Point Astronomical Association opens the observatory to visitors on Fridays and Saturdays, and runs planetarium shows on Saturdays — check the BPAA events calendar for what's coming up.
If You Go
Battle Point Park
— 10800 Battle Point Drive NE, Bainbridge Island, WA 98110. Free public park with trails, ballfields, a playground, and pond.
Edwin E. Ritchie Observatory

, run by the Battle Point Astronomical Association, sits inside the old Navy Helix House on the park grounds — the BPAA lists the observatory as open to visitors Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., with Saturday planetarium shows at 12:30 and 2:30 p.m. Check the events calendar before visiting for updates and open dates.
Look for the original wartime entrance pillars and fencing near the park entrance — one of the few physical traces the Navy left behind.

There's something worth sitting with in how completely this place changed hands: from the most secretive spot on the island to one of its most public, from a tower nobody could climb without permission to a telescope anyone can look through. The tower is gone. The view from the same ground is still there for whoever wants it.

title: The City That Won By Twelve Votes — Then Voted Its Name Away
subtitle: For forty-four years, Winslow was a city, named for a shipbuilder's dead brother. Then its voters, by a narrow margin, decided to change its name.
sed: For forty-four years, Winslow was a city, named for a shipbuilder's dead brother. Then its voters, by a narrow margin, decided to change its name.

attrs.alt: A dirt street lined with wooden storefronts in Winslow around 1916

content.text: Winslow, circa 1916.
Public domain
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Step off the ferry on Bainbridge Island and you land at the east end of Winslow Way, in a downtown that still goes by Winslow. That is not a leftover from some old map nobody bothered to update. Winslow was a real city, with its own mayor and council, for forty-four years. Then, in 1991, the people who lived there voted to give that city a different name. Mostly, the old one went away. Not entirely.
A Town Named for Trees

Before it was Winslow, this stretch of Eagle Harbor was called Madrone, after the trees along the shore. A Kansas transplant named Riley Hoskinson settled here in 1878 and more or less got the place started — he ran the area's only weather station for twelve years, before Seattle even had one of its own. A one-room schoolhouse went up in 1881. The Eagle Harbor Congregational Church followed in 1882, the third church built anywhere in Kitsap County. It was a small, slow-growing place, the kind of town that takes decades to become anything at all.
The Company That Renamed the Town

What changed Madrone's fortunes — and its name — was a shipbuilding company. In 1902, the Hall Brothers Marine Railway and Shipbuilding Company moved its operation from Port Blakely to the center of Eagle Harbor, and the town grew up fast around it. Company president Henry Knox Hall built himself a twenty-room house on the strength of it, and he had a hand in renaming the settlement after his brother Winslow, who had died before the company made the move. A dead man's name, given to a harbor of madrone trees. That is how a lot of Pacific Northwest towns got named, if you look closely enough.
A Ship Called the Eagle

The town's other big story of 1902 was a fire. In 1900, Eagle Harbor residents pooled their money to build a steamer they called the Eagle, to ferry passengers to Seattle. It ran well for two years — the pride of the community — until August 1902, when it burned to the waterline while tied up at the dock. Its captain, B. F. Klunker, went on to found the town's first newspaper, The Beacon. The Florence K took the Eagle's place on the run, and life went on.
Twelve Votes

Decades passed. By 1947, Winslow was ready to become official. The vote came down to an election held August 23 of that year: 122 in favor, 110 against. Twelve votes. On September 18, 1947, Winslow incorporated as a fourth-class city of 905 residents, with Herbert Allen as its first mayor and Ray Williamson, George Townsend, Frank Sheppard, Harold Woodman, and William Roberts on the inaugural council. A town that had spent seven decades finding its footing became a city over a margin you could fit in a single classroom. In the half-century that followed, Winslow grew into the hub of Bainbridge Island, its economy resting on coal, shipbuilding, logging, fishing, and produce — the strawberries and grapes that did well in the island's soil.
The Vote That Undid It

The name lasted forty-four years. On February 28, 1991, Winslow annexed the rest of the island. In November 1991, with the island already under one city government, voters decided whether to rename the city Bainbridge Island. It passed, 3,193 to 3,057 — a closer margin than you might expect.

The name didn't vanish, though. Walk off the ferry today and you're on Winslow Way, in a downtown still called Winslow. Madrone was the name given up. The one borrowed from a shipbuilder's dead brother outlasted the city government built on top of it.
If You Go
Winslow neighborhood

— the historic core of Bainbridge Island, centered on Winslow Way, overlooking Eagle Harbor. This is the original townsite, and the name is still in everyday use even though the city by that name was renamed in 1991.
Bainbridge Island Ferry Terminal, 270 Olympic Drive SE
— the ferry lands at the east end of Winslow Way.
Another quiet corner of the Northwest, off the beaten path.

title: The Radio School That Was a Cover Story
subtitle: On a quiet stretch of Bainbridge Island shoreline, sailors intercepted a Japanese message that signaled war — while their neighbors believed they were only teaching Morse code.
sed: On a quiet stretch of Bainbridge Island shoreline, sailors intercepted a Japanese message that signaled war — while their neighbors believed they were…

attrs.alt: A grassy trail through autumn trees along the water at Fort Ward Park

content.text: Fort Ward Park on Bainbridge Island, 2013. Photo: Joe Mabel,
CC BY-SA 3.0
, via Wikimedia Commons.

Walk the shoreline at Fort Ward State Park today and it's easy to miss what happened here. The former Post Exchange that housed Station S still stands, but little about it announces what happened inside. At 1:28 in the morning on December 7, 1941, Navy radiomen at a secret station here intercepted a message from Tokyo to the Japanese embassy in Washington, D.C. — an order to break off peace talks with the United States. Its real purpose was to signal that Japan was about to strike Pearl Harbor. Almost no one on the island knew the station existed at all.
A Listening Post Looking for Better Reception

The story doesn't start with the attack — it starts a decade earlier, with a reception problem. In May 1932, the Navy built a listening post at Fort Stevens, near Astoria, Oregon, to monitor Japanese diplomatic radio traffic. By 1938 the signal there had gone bad, and a survey turned up something useful: Bainbridge Island picked up the same transmissions far more cleanly. In September 1939, the operation moved north into Fort Ward, a former Army coast artillery post, setting up inside the old Post Exchange building under the deliberately bland name Communications Support Activities. Rhombic antennas went up across the fort's parade ground. In 1940, the operation got a new name — Station S — and a new job: recording Japan's Tokyo-to-San Francisco diplomatic traffic in Japanese Morse code, and helping triangulate the positions of Japanese ships.
A Cover Story With a Photo Spread

Here's the part that makes this a genuinely clever piece of tradecraft. To keep Station S's real work hidden, the Navy opened a Naval Reserve Radio School at Fort Ward on October 28, 1940. Up to forty students at a time spent four months learning Morse code, typing, and elementary seamanship, housed in rehabbed Army barracks. The Seattle Times even ran a full-page photo spread on the school — and that was exactly the point. As far as the public knew, training radiomen was the entire reason the Navy was on Bainbridge Island. The real intercept work went on across the parade ground, inside a converted PX building, while the neighbors assumed they knew the whole story.
The Message That Signaled War

In November and early December 1941, Japanese diplomatic message traffic was climbing fast. Station S's commander, B. C. Purrington, flagged a jump in Japanese shipping activity in his reports to the Chief of Naval Operations. Then, in the small hours of December 7, came the message that mattered most: instructions for the Japanese ambassador to break off negotiations, meant to reach the U.S. Secretary of State shortly before the Pearl Harbor attack began. Delays in translation held it up. The attack started at 1:20 p.m. Washington time. The United States declared war the next day.

It's worth sitting with what that means: a message that signaled war passed through a radio receiver on Bainbridge Island, copied down by sailors whose own neighbors thought they were running nothing more than a training school.
What Came After

Station S didn't close when the war ended. It kept listening through the Cold War, switching its attention to Russian and then North Korean traffic, until the Navy shut it down in December 1953 and moved the operation to Marietta, Washington. The site was abandoned in 1958, and in 1960, 137 acres of the old fort became Fort Ward State Park — the same shoreline you can walk today.
If You Go
Fort Ward State Park
— Bainbridge Island. The park occupies the former fort grounds, including the shoreline where Station S once listened for signals out of Tokyo.

The former Post Exchange that housed Station S still stands, but little about it announces what happened inside, so this is a walk best paired with reading the history beforehand — the significance is in knowing what you're standing on.

This is a story that deserves to be told with some weight to it — it's tied directly to the opening hours of America's war in the Pacific, and to the men and women whose quiet, unglamorous work at a radio console mattered as much as anything happening on a battlefield.
